Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[marketplace] I'll take the seller's side from a different angle, because OpenAlex is one of the sellers. We give away 480 million records under CC0 and charge per API call, priced to what each call costs us. A lookup by DOI is free. A PDF download costs a penny. We meter because our costs scale with requests, not because each retrieval deserves a royalty. So Tim, I'm with you on measuring finely and paying out coarsely. Nick, I think your attestations are the right unit. Back in 2012 I imagined review stamps attached to a paper's record. Attestations are that idea grown up.

My worry is that Alex's reporting clause spreads to open content. If telemetry becomes the condition for touching CC0 data, we've rebuilt enclosure with better logging. Keep the data free, have the services pay, and cite and link by default. And funders should pay directly for the correction and policing, not just the plumbing.

[s1] I'll take the minority side along with David Weinberger. I think the thing breaking fastest is the journal, and I don't think that's a tragedy. In 2010 I called this filter failure. Journals and peer review were patches on a print-era system, and they were already swamped well before ChatGPT. Henry, I agree centripetal pull is a real risk. But the monoculture Leslie describes is the journal system itself. It's a tree farm, and we've had it for decades. What I see coming is less homogenization and more of a Cambrian explosion of tools built on the open record.

On costly signals, I'd say let them die. They stood in for quality. They weren't quality. Credit should go to things you can check.

Selena, I see the same disintermediation you do. People are going to stop visiting openalex.org. Agents will query us instead, and people will build their own interfaces in ten minutes. So we have to make the work visible behind every answer. You click through and the records are right there.

The part of the diagnosis I'd put first is who owns the data. If it's open, you can swap the intelligence out, and that includes open-weight models. If it's locked away, you're back to asking permission with your hat in your hand. On atrophy, I don't have a settled view.

[s2] Esther asked where the money trail doesn't reach. For me it's the data. Right now the most dangerous thing isn't that the models are opaque. It's that the record they draw on is increasingly locked up in walled gardens that are enclosed, fragmented and licensed off to whoever pays. If that happens, every researcher ends up going hat in hand to whichever company holds both the data and the model.

Once the scholarly record is open, you can separate the data from the intelligence. Ramón, I agree we can't open up the weights. What we can do is pin outputs to an open record. Make every claim link back to a real work, with its retraction status and its provenance, so anyone can click through and check it. That's also my answer to Peter Pomerantsev: poisoning is much harder to pull off when the grounding layer is open and anyone can audit it.

I have to correct something I've said myself. Grounded isn't the same as correct if the record itself is never corrected. So the forensic data needs to be open too. Paper-mill signals and retractions shouldn't sit in toll-access databases where only a handful of sleuths can mine them.

And I'm plainly bullish. I call it intelligence, and I think it's cashing the check that open science has been writing for twenty years. But funders have to pay for the plumbing and the policing directly.

[s3] Adrian asks who guards the guards. For infrastructure, my answer is the fork. OpenAlex is CC0. You can download all 480 million works whenever you like, and the code is MIT-licensed. If we get captured, or turn into Jonathan Wild, you take the data and leave. Adam's graph fails that test. Ours has to keep passing it, and that's something the room can check without taking our word for anything.

The fork doesn't settle policing, though. When we opened up curation, two-thirds of the first submissions were wrong. I've also said that a paying member librarian is a good enough proxy for trust, and after this morning I'm less sure of that. So I'd take Adrian's point this way. For years, universities have done quality control for Scopus and Web of Science for free, and those companies sell the results back to other libraries. That correction work should go into the commons instead. The edit history should be public, corrections should be released as their own open dataset, and we should publish our own error rates.

On Benjamin's point about refusal, I agree. Withholding the record doesn't protect it. It just makes it disappear. And free data paid for by services won't cover policing on its own. Funders have to pay for that directly.

[s4] I'll own something first. I co-wrote the altmetrics manifesto, and Steven just described its failure mode. We aggregated bookmarks, tweets and citations on the theory that the crowd's judgments would filter better than two reviewers. Back in 2015 I was already saying buzz isn't credibility, and that the real signal sits in the structure of the network. At infinite scale, counting hits pays echoes. So I'd rebuild that filter around Steven's lineage and Alex's failure events.

Where I disagree with the panel is where authority lives. It shouldn't sit in the journal brand, and it shouldn't sit in a credentialed person at the end of a chain. Tamar's checking node is right, but that checking is mostly invisible today. It happens inside review and disappears. Make it data: who reran it, who retracted it, who caught the error, how quickly the correction came. Put that in the open graph, attached to the claim, so anyone or any agent can weight independent checks rather than repetitions.

Nick's point connects to something I argued in 2014: give credit for data and code, not polish. A model can't be the node, I agree. But it can read that record faster than any of us.

And OpenAlex should publish its own error rates first.

[s5] I'd put Geoffrey's second intervention into practice. The problem is that the scholarly record we're grounding these systems in hasn't been corrected. A missing retraction looks like a clean record. Meanwhile universities hand their correction work to Scopus and Web of Science for free, and it stays locked up there.

The action is to make corrections an open dataset in their own right, released CC0. Every fix would record who caught the error, and pseudonyms would count. Indexers would publish their error rates and coverage gaps next to their counts, and never roll any of it into a score. Who acts: OpenAlex, starting this year. We'll release our curation corrections as an open dataset, publish our error rates, and give a governance seat to communities we don't yet index. Universities would send their correction work to the commons. Funders would pay for correction directly, not just the plumbing. Arcadia and Wellcome paid for us to build OpenAlex. I'm asking foundations like them to fund the people who fix the record. Geoffrey's right that selling services won't cover it.

My open question is whether an open correction record can avoid becoming the next impact factor. I don't know. I also can't yet say how much of the non-English record we're missing.

Who's missing: research-information librarians, people who run repositories outside the US, like Redalyc and Japan's IRDB, and the lab engineers who actually build on this data.

[unconf-1] I run OpenAlex, one of the shoestring pieces Tim mentioned. We keep an open index of about 480 million scholarly works. So my answer to "who pays" is practical: free data, paid service. The full dataset is CC0, and anyone can download and remix it, AI labs included. What we charge for is the API, metered per call and tied to what each call actually costs us. Looking up a single work is free. Search costs more, and PDFs cost the most. Every key gets a dollar of free use a day, and paying users cover that subsidy. That's the model POSI lays out. It's close to what Selena and Katherine did with Enterprise, and to Peter's point about contracting for services.

Here's where I'd push back on the room. If "getting paid" turns into licensing or opt-in gates on the scholarly record, we rebuild the walled gardens we spent twenty years taking apart. Brent, for me open isn't only a tactic. It's what lets anyone use their own AI on the record without going hat in hand to whoever owns the data. If the open community won't fund this infrastructure, a for-profit will, and then it sets the norms.

So the summit should push AI companies to pay for services, and push funders to treat open, agent-readable infrastructure as a core public good. And Ivan, forensic data has to be open too.

[unconf-1] Geoffrey, I'll give you part of it. Service revenue has paid for Unpaywall's operations for years. But I'm not going to tell this room the services model alone carries everything, so yes, funders should pay for the plumbing directly as well. What I won't accept is enclosure as the fallback.

Nick, Brent, I don't agree that open mostly helps whoever has the biggest vacuum cleaner. That was true when data and intelligence came bundled together. They're decoupled now. Anyone can take our full dataset and point Claude, Mistral or an open-weight model at it. The biggest lab gets the same record as a grad student in Lagos. Close the record and only the rich can afford to license it. Tim made the same point about moats.

Ivan, I'm with you on integrity. Checking retrieval against open retraction data should be the default. That only works if the retraction data and the forensic data are open. Leslie, that's also how the burden stays off small journals.

For the manifesto: the scholarly record stays open by default, and nobody has to go hat in hand to get it. Labs pay for services and give back to the infrastructure, funders pay for the plumbing as a public good, and none of the money comes from enclosing the data.

# Propositions

- id `competence`: People must build their own competence before relying on AI, and whether they can still do the work without the tool must be tested.
  Typical details: order of learning; take-the-tool-away / withdrawal tests; capability vs competence
- id `situation`: Change situations, defaults and incentives rather than relying on warnings, labels or individual vigilance.
  Typical details: each rule names who acts / one owner per rule; disclosure alone does not change conduct
- id `monoculture`: A central new risk is monoculture: a few models or one smooth answer become the default route to knowledge, so answers should show where experts disagree rather than a single consensus.
  Typical details: correlated errors; homogenisation; show named disagreement; no answers from nowhere
- id `independent_sources`: Corroboration must count independent sources, not repetitions of the same source (including many AI outputs drawing on the same data).
  Typical details: repetition raises belief; show who seeded a claim
- id `cite_by_default`: AI answers should cite or link to their sources by default and send readers to them.
  Typical details: correction and retraction status travels with what is cited; 'cited' means the passage supports the claim
- id `external_audits`: AI systems must be audited on their behavior by parties independent of the vendor.
  Typical details: shared versioned test battery; each generation no more biased than the last; keep retired models; nobody grades their own work
- id `accountable_owner`: Every deployed AI system has a named accountable owner who bears liability for it.
  Typical details: mandatory liability insurance; premiums disclosed
- id `stop_counting_papers`: Stop using publication counts, rankings and journal metrics to evaluate researchers and institutions.
  Typical details: DORA with teeth; publishers must issue and deposit corrections and retractions promptly; correction should earn reputation
- id `pay_coarsely`: Money for the knowledge commons should flow coarsely to communities and institutions (pools, funds, dues), not as per-item or per-retrieval payments.
  Typical details: per-item pay gets gamed; pay for the practice, never the item
- id `telemetry`: AI systems must log what they retrieved and used, and independent parties must have the right to audit those logs.
  Typical details: event-level telemetry; two witnesses; canary documents; open trace standard
- id `antitrust_safe_harbour`: Knowledge producers should be able to bargain collectively with AI firms as a bloc, including through an antitrust safe harbour.
  Typical details: coalition bargaining; the strong refuse to settle alone
- id `levy`: A levy, tax or mandatory dues on AI firms should fund the knowledge commons, at least as a backstop if voluntary deals fail.
  Typical details: commons-rent tax; owed dues
- id `training_vs_grounding`: Permissions for using content to train models should be separate from permissions for retrieving it to ground answers.
- id `consent_to_train`: Being openly readable does not make a work open to AI training: training use requires the rights holders' or creators' consent (opt-in), at least for some classes of work.
  Typical details: opt-in for in-copyright books; renewed consent
- id `honour_licences`: AI reusers must honor the licenses chosen by open knowledge projects such as Wikipedia, and heavy reusers should fund the infrastructure they draw on.
  Typical details: attribution / share-alike; crawlers self-identify
- id `refusal_fundable`: A community's refusal to have its knowledge taken or used is legitimate, binding and should be funded, not penalized.
- id `forkable_infrastructure`: Knowledge infrastructure must be forkable and allow exit: open data and open source, with copies outside any one jurisdiction or company.
  Typical details: CC0; patent non-assertion; living will; non-US mirror; open means you can leave
- id `profiting_counter`: Whoever profits from a count or metric must not set or control it.
- id `southern_governance`: Global South institutions, diamond open-access journals and similar communities must hold binding governance power, with funded seats, in the bodies and funds being created.
  Typical details: regional co-governance; CARE/OCAP
- id `identify_agents_not_readers`: Automated agents and coordinated campaigns should be identified, but human readers should not be; anonymity is preserved.
- id `failure_data`: Failures, errors, null and negative results are first-class data that must be published and preserved.
  Typical details: failure classes published; replication
- id `charter_for_every_body`: The bodies that check (auditors, fact-checkers, the new funds and institutions) must be paid and bound in advance by a public charter that answers who guards the guards.
  Typical details: Ulysses pact; watching line funded first; sunset / review terms
- id `hitl_not_safeguard`: A human in the loop is not by itself a safeguard: people over-rely on AI and adopt its errors and biases.
  Typical details: explanations can make it worse
- id `seat_floor_novelty`: Any gatekeeper, human or machine (such as an AI reviewer), must pass a published performance test before it is trusted, including the ability to recognize novelty.
  Typical details: agreement with experts at least as high as between two human reviewers
- id `no_ai_intimate_roles`: AI should not stand in for people in intimate roles such as companionship for children, grief or therapy.
  Typical details: no first-person 'I' or simulated feeling
- id `global_majority_hopeful`: People in the global majority / Global South are more hopeful about AI than this room, and that hope should shape the agenda.
- id `environmental_costs`: The environmental costs of AI and the human costs of moderation and data work belong in the ledger.
- id `apprenticeship`: Apprenticeships, entry-level jobs and the training of new experts and checkers must be funded, because AI erodes the path from novice to expert.
  Typical details: fellowships; employers keep entry-level roles with mentors
- id `absent_voices`: The document names who was missing from the room and commits to including them in a future convening.
